343.title: Solutions, colloids, and suspensions differ in appearance and in how they treat light

members.title: Solutions, colloids, and suspensions differ in appearance and in how they treat light
members.content: The illustration shows three distinct types of mixtures: a solution, a colloid, and a suspension. In the first image, a solution is depicted as a uniform and clear liquid, with light passing straight through it and the particles within it being too small to be seen or settle. The second image shows a colloid, where light is scattered inside the mixture, and the particles do not separate when the mixture is left undisturbed, like gatas, taho, or mayonesa. Finally, the third image represents a suspension, which is cloudy and the solid particles settle at the bottom when it is left undisturbed, such as muddy water or gawgaw in water, and light is blocked.

members.title: Uniform and Non-Uniform Mixtures (Part 1 of 3)
members.content:
The Grade 6 competency asks learners to sort mixtures by appearance.
The question is simple: does A uniform mixture, also called a homogeneous mixture, looks the same in every part.
The components are so evenly spread that you cannot tell them apart by looking.

members.title: Uniform and Non-Uniform Mixtures (Part 2 of 3)
members.content:
A glass of sugar water, a cup of brewed coffee without grounds, and a sip of buko juice all look like a single liquid, even though each one contains several materials.
Uniform mixtures of this kind are called solutions.
A non-uniform mixture, also called a heterogeneous mixture, shows its components.

members.title: Uniform and Non-Uniform Mixtures (Part 3 of 3)
members.content:
You can see the separate parts, and different spoonfuls may not look the same.
A bowl of halo-halo, a plate of pancit, a handful of rice mixed with corn, and a glass of muddy water are all non-uniform.

members.title: Solutions: Solute and Solvent
members.content:
In a solution, the material that dissolves is the solute, and the material that does the dissolving is the solvent. In sweetened coffee, the sugar is the solute and the hot water is the solvent. The solvent is usually the component present in the greater amount, and water is so common as a solvent that it is often called the universal solvent.
Three conditions affect how quickly a solute dissolves, and learners can test each one:
Size of the particles. Finely ground sugar dissolves faster than a large lump, because more of its surface touches the water.
Stirring. A stirred glass dissolves its sugar faster than one left standing, because stirring keeps bringing fresh water into contact with the solute.
Temperature. Sugar dissolves faster in hot water than in cold water, which is why powdered drinks mix easily in warm water but leave grains at the bottom of a cold glass.
Not every solute dissolves in every solvent. Salt and sugar dissolve in water, but cooking oil does not.
Oil and water separate into two layers no matter how long they are stirred, which is why a bottle of salad dressing must be shaken before use.

members.title: Suspensions and Colloids (Part 1 of 3)
members.content:
Between the clear solution and the obviously separated mixture are two kinds worth naming.
A suspension is a non-uniform mixture in which solid particles are large enough to be seen and heavy enough to settle when the mixture is left alone.

members.title: Suspensions and Colloids (Part 2 of 3)
members.content:
Gawgaw stirred into water, muddy water from a flooded street, and a bottle of medicine labelled "shake well before using" are all suspensions.
Their particles can be trapped by filter paper.
A colloid sits in between.

members.title: Suspensions and Colloids (Part 3 of 3)
members.content:
Its particles are too small to settle out, so the mixture stays evenly cloudy for a long time, but they are still large enough to scatter light.
Gatas, taho, mayonesa, gulaman, and the smoke from burning leaves are colloids.

members.title: Air as a Mixture (Part 1 of 2)
members.content:
Not all mixtures are liquids.
Air is a mixture of gases, and the Grade 6 competency names its main components: nitrogen, which makes up the largest share; oxygen, which living things need for respiration; carbon dioxide, which plants use to make food; and water vapor, whose amount rises and falls with the weather.

members.title: Air as a Mixture (Part 2 of 2)
members.content:
Air is a uniform mixture: it looks the same throughout, and its gases do not settle into layers.
Because the components are only physically combined, each keeps its own properties — which is why oxygen can still support burning even while it is mixed with the other gases.

357.title: The main parts of a flower involved in reproduction

members.title: The main parts of a flower involved in reproduction
members.content: The image shows the key components of a flower involved in reproduction. At the top, the stamen is positioned first, consisting of a filament supporting an anther, which produces pollen. Below the stamen is the pistil, comprising the ovary and style, with the style leading to an ovule within the ovary, where egg cells are stored. The petals and sepals surround these central parts of the flower, providing protection and attracting pollinators.

members.title: The main parts of a flower involved in reproduction
members.content: The image shows a flower with several distinct parts arranged around a central core. At the top, there are multiple, slender stalks, called filaments, supporting a cluster of small, rounded structures – these are the anthers, which produce pollen. Below the anthers, and extending downwards, is a central, elongated structure – the pistil – which is composed of a sticky, top part called the stigma, and a shorter, tube-like section known as the style. At the base of the pistil is a swollen, rounded structure called the ovary, which contains the egg cells.

members.title: Reproduction in Flowering Plants
members.content: Flowering plants reproduce sexually, which means a new plant begins when a male sex cell joins a female sex cell. Most of this activity happens inside the flower, which is the reproductive part of the plant. A single flower can contain both male and female parts, and these parts work together so that seeds can form. Seeds later grow into new plants, allowing the species to continue.

members.title: Reproduction in Flowering Plants (Part 1 of 2)
members.content:
Flowering plants reproduce sexually, which means a new plant begins when a male sex cell joins a female sex cell.
Most of this activity happens inside the flower, which is the reproductive part of the plant.

members.title: Reproduction in Flowering Plants (Part 2 of 2)
members.content:
A single flower can contain both male and female parts, and these parts work together so that seeds can form.
Seeds later grow into new plants, allowing the species to continue.
Male parts (the stamen) produce pollen; female parts (the pistil) hold the egg cells.

members.title: Stamen (Male Part)
members.content: The stamen is made up of the anther and the filament. The filament is the thin stalk that holds up the anther, while the anther produces tiny grains called pollen. Each pollen grain carries a male sex cell.

members.title: Stamen (Male Part)
members.content: The stamen is made up of the anther and the filament. The filament is the thin stalk that holds up the anther, while the anther produces tiny grains called pollen. Each pollen grain carries a male sex cell.

members.title: Pistil (Female Part)
members.content: The pistil, also called the carpel, is made up of the stigma, style, and ovary. The sticky stigma catches pollen, the style connects the stigma to the ovary, and the ovary contains ovules. Each ovule holds a female sex cell, or egg.

members.title: Pistil (Female Part)
members.content: The pistil, also called the carpel, is made up of the stigma, style, and ovary. The sticky stigma catches pollen, the style connects the stigma to the ovary, and the ovary contains ovules. Each ovule holds a female sex cell, or egg.

members.title: Petals and Sepals (Supporting Parts)
members.content:
The colorful petals attract pollinators such as bees, butterflies, and birds. The green sepals protect the flower while it is still a bud.
These parts do not make sex cells, but they help reproduction succeed.

members.title: Petals and Sepals (Supporting Parts)
members.content: The colorful petals attract pollinators such as bees, butterflies, and birds. The green sepals protect the flower while it is still a bud. These parts do not make sex cells, but they help reproduction succeed.

members.title: Pollination
members.content: Pollen is carried from the anther to the stigma. This can happen within the same flower or between different flowers, with the help of wind, water, insects, or other animals.

members.title: Pollination
members.content: Pollen is carried from the anther to the stigma. This can happen within the same flower or between different flowers, with the help of wind, water, insects, or other animals.

members.title: Fertilization
members.content: After landing on the stigma, a pollen grain grows a tube down the style into the ovary. The male sex cell then joins the egg cell inside an ovule.

members.title: Fertilization
members.content: After landing on the stigma, a pollen grain grows a tube down the style into the ovary. The male sex cell then joins the egg cell inside an ovule.

members.title: Seed formation
members.content: The fertilized ovule develops into a seed, which contains a tiny young plant and a store of food.

members.title: Seed formation
members.content: The fertilized ovule develops into a seed, which contains a tiny young plant and a store of food.

members.title: Fruit formation
members.content: The ovary grows into a fruit that surrounds and protects the seeds and helps them spread to new places.

members.title: Everyday Examples
members.content: A gumamela (hibiscus) shows all the flower parts clearly, which is why it is often used in class. A mango tree flowers, is pollinated, and then forms the mango fruit with a seed inside. Rice plants are pollinated mostly by wind, while many fruit trees depend on bees. These examples show that pollination and fertilization must happen first before a seed or fruit can form, and each seed carries the beginnings of a brand-new plant.
